# Fixed-mass John contact graphs and strict concavity in the base

This note proves a graph lemma and a stronger property specific to fixed-mass
moment bodies. It does not assert a halfspace-depth bound at a John center.
The continuous dimension is `d>=1`, and the source uses full-dimensional
Lebesgue measure in each of finitely many integer fibers. No intrinsic
lower-dimensional extension is implicit.

## 1. The joint fixed-mass moment body

Let `mu=sum_(z in P) delta_z tensor 1_(K_z) dx`, where `P` is finite,
each `K_z subset R^d` is a compact convex body, and the lifted fibers
are the actual integer fibers of their convex hull. Let `M=mu(S)`.
Fix `0<t<=M`, and define

    B_t={(t^(-1) integral z f dmu, t^(-1) integral x f dmu):
                       0<=f<=1, integral f dmu=t}.

This is a compact convex set: the density interval is weak-star compact
in `L^infinity(mu)`, and all mass and coordinate integrals are continuous
on it because the support is bounded. Let `Q_t` be its base projection.
Its section at any real `j in Q_t` is exactly

    M_t(j)={t^(-1) integral x f dmu:
                    0<=f<=1, integral f=t, integral z f=tj}.

The joint graph is therefore convex, and for real feasible bases

    (1-lambda)M_t(j_1)+lambda M_t(j_2)
       subset M_t((1-lambda)j_1+lambda j_2).          (1)

Every point of `B_t` belongs to the original convex hull by the
barycenter property. In particular an integer section of `B_t` lies
in the actual original fiber. There are finitely many feasible integer
bases because `Q_t` is bounded.

## 2. A density-slack lemma giving strict vertical compatibility

**Lemma.** Suppose `f` is feasible at mass `t` and there is a positive-
measure subset `A` of one source fiber on which
`delta<=f<=1-delta` for some `delta>0`. Then its continuous barycenter
is an interior point of the section `M_t(j)` at its own base barycenter.

**Proof.** Regard `A` as a bounded positive-Lebesgue-measure subset of
`R^d`. Write its volume as `v`, its centroid as `a`, and its covariance
matrix as

    Sigma=(1/v) integral_A (x-a)(x-a)^T dx.

This matrix is positive definite: a zero quadratic form in a nonzero
direction would place almost all of `A` in a hyperplane, impossible
for positive `d`-dimensional measure. For a vector `b`, put

    psi_b(x)=1_A(x) b^T Sigma^(-1)(x-a)/v.

Then `integral psi_b=0` and `integral x psi_b=b`. Boundedness of `A`
gives `||psi_b||_infinity<=C|b|` for a finite constant `C`. For small
enough `b`, replacing `f` by `f+psi_b` on this one fiber keeps it
between zero and one. It preserves total mass and all base moments,
while moving the continuous barycenter by `b/t`. This proves the lemma.

If two feasible densities `f_1,f_2` differ on a positive-measure set,
every strict convex mixture of them has the slack required in the
lemma. Indeed, where their values differ, their strict mixture lies
strictly between zero and one. A finite fiber and one positive level
`delta` can be selected from this set by countable exhaustion.

Consequently, for DISTINCT real bases `j_1,j_2` and `0<lambda<1`,

    (1-lambda)M_t(j_1)+lambda M_t(j_2)
       subset int M_t((1-lambda)j_1+lambda j_2).     (2)

To check this for any represented pair, their densities cannot agree
almost everywhere because their base barycenters differ. The slack
lemma applies to the mixture. The inclusion concerns the full
continuous interior and not merely a relative interior.

The same argument proves a useful degeneracy dichotomy: every nonempty
section `M_t(j)` is either a singleton or a full-dimensional body. If
it had two distinct points, their represented densities would differ,
and their midpoint would have a full continuous neighborhood. In fact
any nontrivial segment between two points of a section has its relative
interior in the full interior of the section. This assertion does not
require support-dual attainment at boundary mass.

## 3. John ellipsoids: existence, uniqueness, and the determinant inequality

For a full-dimensional compact convex set `K subset R^d`, write a
largest inscribed ellipsoid as `c+A B_d`, with `A` symmetric positive
definite. Existence follows by allowing positive semidefinite shape
matrices: all centers and operator norms are bounded by containment,
the feasible set is closed, and determinant is continuous. An inball
makes the maximum determinant positive.

For positive definite matrices, the determinant-root inequality is

    det((1-lambda)A+lambda B)^(1/d)
       >=(1-lambda)det(A)^(1/d)+lambda det(B)^(1/d). (3)

Here is an elementary verification. Conjugate by `A^(-1/2)` and let
the resulting positive eigenvalues of `B` be `s_1,...,s_d`. Expanding
`product((1-lambda)+lambda s_i)`, each elementary symmetric coefficient
is at least its binomial coefficient times
`(product s_i)^(k/d)`, by arithmetic-geometric mean applied to the
products over all `k`-element subsets. Their sum is
`((1-lambda)+lambda(product s_i)^(1/d))^d`. This proves (3).
For `0<lambda<1`, equality requires all `s_i` equal when `d>=2`, by
the coefficient with `k=1`; thus the matrices are proportional.
For `d=1` positive scalar matrices are already proportional.
The finite weighted version follows by induction, with equality only
when all positive-weight matrices are proportional.

The maximum inscribed ellipsoid is unique. If two maximizing shapes
differ, (3) applied to their midpoint ellipsoid, contained in their
Minkowski average, increases volume unless their shapes are
proportional. Equal volume then makes the shapes equal. If their
centers differ while the shape is the same, normalize that shape to
the unit ball and their centers to `+-v`, `v!=0`. The convex hull
contains `B_d+[-v,v]`, which contains the ellipsoid with shape
`(I+v v^T)^(1/2)`: its support value
`sqrt(|u|^2+(u.v)^2)` is at most `|u|+|u.v|`. This ellipsoid has
volume multiplier `sqrt(1+|v|^2)>1`, a contradiction. This proves
uniqueness without identifying the body with its ellipsoid.

## 4. A general maximum-John-volume graph lemma

First let `B subset R^n x R^d` be ANY compact convex set having at
least one integer section with positive John volume. For each such
section write its John ellipsoid as `E_j=c_j+A_j B_d`, and let
`J_j=vol_d(E_j)`. Put `J_j=0` for a lower-dimensional nonempty section.
Let `J_*>0` be the maximum over its finitely many integer sections,
and let `E` be the maximizing base indices.

Suppose a positive convex combination of indices of `E` has integer
average `w`. Convexity gives an inscribed ellipsoid of the target
section with center `sum lambda_j c_j` and shape `sum lambda_j A_j`.
By (3) its volume is at least `J_*`. By maximality it is exactly
`J_*`, and `w` is another maximizing index. Equality in (3), together
with equal determinant of the source matrices, makes all `A_j` equal.
Uniqueness of the target John ellipsoid then gives

    sum lambda_j c_j=c_w.

Therefore

    conv{(j,c_j):j in E} intersect (Z^n x R^d)
       ={(j,c_j):j in E}.                            (4)

Strict containment of an ellipsoid in parts of its ambient body does
not obstruct this argument. It is uniqueness of the maximizing
ellipsoid, not equality of body volumes, that gives the center identity.

The same proof applies to positive contacts of a GLOBAL affine majorant
of `J_j^(1/d)` on the feasible integer indices. The source ellipsoids
are then positively homothetic, and their Minkowski-average ellipsoid
is the unique target John ellipsoid. The global-majorant assumption
is essential to this contact version.

## 5. The stronger fixed-mass conclusion

For the specific joint moment body `B_t`, define `J_t(j)` on every
feasible real base to be its section's John volume if it is a body,
and zero if it is a singleton. Put `rho_t(j)=J_t(j)^(1/d)`.
Then `rho_t` is STRICTLY concave across any two distinct feasible
real bases.

If both endpoint sections have positive John volume, their ellipsoid
Minkowski average is a compact subset of the target section's interior
by (2). It contains the ellipsoid with averaged center and shape
`(1-lambda)A_1+lambda A_2`. That ellipsoid can be dilated by a factor
strictly larger than one while remaining in the target section:
compact containment supplies a positive distance to the complement.
Combining this strict improvement with (3) gives

    rho_t((1-lambda)j_1+lambda j_2)
       >(1-lambda)rho_t(j_1)+lambda rho_t(j_2).       (5)

If one endpoint section is a singleton, use that point and the other
ellipsoid; its averaged shape is still positive definite and the same
argument proves (5). If both are singletons, (2) gives a positive-volume
target section, also proving (5).

Assume at least one feasible integer section has positive John volume,
and maximize `J_t(j)` over the feasible integer bases. If distinct
maximizing indices had an integer convex average, strict concavity
would make the target value larger. Hence such an average is impossible.
The maximizing set is in convex position, has no other lattice point
in its convex hull, and contains at most one representative of each
parity class. In particular

    number of maximizing integer bases <=2^n.       (6)

Their John-center graph has the singleton integer sections in (4).
In fact the same singleton graph assertion holds for ANY values assigned
to this base set, since its only integer convex representations are
the trivial ones. Every positive global affine-majorant contact set of
`rho_t` has the same no-integer-average property and the same bound (6).

The positivity assumption cannot simply be omitted from a definition of
a full-dimensional John ellipsoid. A sufficient condition is
`0<t<T_max(j)` at some original integer fiber: mixing a maximum balanced
source with a smaller strictly feasible source gives density slack and
hence a positive moment-body inball. In particular `t<w_j` suffices.
If no integer section is feasible there is no graph to select. If
integer sections are feasible but all their John volumes are zero,
they are singletons by Section 2. Strictness (5) still excludes a
nontrivial integer average among them, so their singleton graph and
parity cardinality bound remain valid as a separate zero-volume case.

## 6. Actual contact sources and their weights

Fix a positive section and its John ellipsoid `c+A B_d`. Its normalized
John contact vectors and weights satisfy

    sum_s lambda_s v_s=0,
    sum_s lambda_s v_s v_s^T=I_d,
    sum_s lambda_s=d,

with positive weights and at most `d+d(d+1)/2` contacts. The finite
separation proof is recorded in `candidate 0ca1f875b898090e`.
Every contact point `c+A v_s` belongs to `M_t(j)`, so choose an actual
feasible dominated source density `f_s` representing it. Then

    f_c=(1/d)sum_s lambda_s f_s

is dominated by one, has mass `t`, base centroid exactly `j`, and
continuous centroid exactly `c`. The weights here sum to one after
division by `d`. The covariance of the CONTACT CENTROIDS under these
weights is `A^2/d`. The covariance of the source itself additionally
contains the within-source covariance terms; they are not discarded.
In full ambient coordinates, with `sigma_s=f_s mu`, `sigma_c=f_c mu`
and all component covariances taken under their normalized probability
laws, the exact identity is

    Cov_(sigma_c/t)(z,x)
       =(1/d)sum_s lambda_s Cov_(sigma_s/t)(z,x)
          + [[0_(n x n), 0], [0, A^2/d]].

Thus all source integer-coordinate covariances and all mixed cross
moments remain in the first term. Only the between-component centroid
covariance has zero integer blocks, because every component's integer
centroid is the same `j`.

If `0<t<T_max(j)`, the attained-dual result in that note permits each
`f_s` to be its unique actual cap indicator, with continuous normal
`u_s=A^(-1)v_s`, mass `t`, and base centroid `j`. At boundary mass,
the feasible source representation above is still attained by moment
compactness, but this note makes no unsupported assertion that every
such source has an attained finite cap tilt.

Writing its fiber masses as `m_(z,s)=integral_(K_z) f_s dx`, the exact
constraints are `sum_z m_(z,s)=t` and `sum_z z m_(z,s)=tj`. They do
NOT say that these sources are concentrated in the fiber `j`. Nor
does John balance cancel the associated integer tilt coefficients.
The explicit nonzero coefficient in the cited source-dual note remains
an obstruction; none of the graph statements removes it.

## 7. Lattice, mass, ellipsoid, and dual-coordinate bookkeeping

An allowed invertible mixed-affine transformation has form

    z'=U z+b,       x'=L x+B z+c,

where `U` is unimodular, `b` is integer, `L` is an invertible real
`d x d` matrix, and the remaining coefficients are real. Set
`Delta=|det L|`. Ordinary mixed volume on the transformed fibers is
`mu'=Delta T_#mu`. Thus the corresponding fixed mass is
`t'=Delta t`, and `B'_(t')=T(B_t)`. Keeping instead the pushed-forward
measure `T_#mu` would keep `t` and insert the density factor
`1/Delta`; these two conventions are not interchangeable.

At `j'=Uj+b`, the John center becomes `Lc_j+Bj+c`, the ellipsoid is
the image of the original one, and its canonical positive definite
shape matrix is

    A'_j=(L A_j^2 L^T)^(1/2).

Its volume is `Delta J_j`, and its volume root is
`Delta^(1/d)rho_j`; maximizing index sets and all graph conclusions
transform accordingly. The normalized contact vectors transform by
the orthogonal matrix `O=(A'_j)^(-1)L A_j`, with unchanged weights.
Their raw continuous normals transform as `u'_s=L^(-T)u_s`.

For an attained cap written as

    u_s.x+a_s.(z-j)-beta_s>=0,

the corresponding coefficients are

    a'_s=U^(-T)(a_s-B^T u'_s),
    beta'_s=beta_s+u'_s.(Bj+c).

Since `sum lambda_s u'_s=0`, the aggregate integer term satisfies

    sum lambda_s a'_s=U^(-T)sum lambda_s a_s.

In particular a nonzero aggregate integer term cannot be eliminated
by one of these allowed fiber shears or unimodular normalizations.
The aggregate threshold is unchanged, and hinge integrals and source
masses both scale by `Delta`.

These exact identities provide a deterministic contact-center graph
and strong base strictness. They do not convert a John-center source
representation into an OC cap-depth guarantee.

## 8. The surviving integer term supports the John-volume root

There is a precise global meaning to that integer term. Assume
`0<t<T_max(j)` so the actual support caps in Section 6 attain, and
put `bar a=sum_s lambda_s a_s`, using the John-normalized continuous
normals there. Then for EVERY real feasible base `j' in Q_t`,

    rho_t(j') <= rho_t(j)
                  [1-(bar a/d).(j'-j)].              (7)

Thus `-rho_t(j) bar a/d` is an actual concave supergradient of the
John-volume root, not merely an unconstrained collection of integer
coefficients.

To prove this, the fixed source cap dual is valid for every mass-`t`
source, whether or not its base mean equals `j`. It gives

    h_(M_t(j'))(u_s)
       <=h_(M_t(j))(u_s)-a_s.(j'-j).

Normalize the original John ellipsoid to the unit ball. If the target
section has positive John shape `H` and normalized center `b`, the
last inequalities become

    v_s.b+|H v_s| <=1-a_s.(j'-j).

Here `H` is the canonical symmetric positive definite shape in the
normalized coordinates, so `det(H)^(1/d)=rho_t(j')/rho_t(j)`.
Multiply by the John weights and sum. Their vector balance removes
the center, and their matrix balance gives

    tr(H)=sum_s lambda_s v_s^T H v_s
         <=sum_s lambda_s |H v_s|
         <=d-bar a.(j'-j).

Arithmetic-geometric mean of the eigenvalues gives
`det(H)^(1/d)<=tr(H)/d`, proving (7). If the target section is a
singleton, use its normalized center and zero shape in the same
contact inequalities; their sum says the right side of (7) is
nonnegative, which is exactly the needed bound for `rho_t(j')=0`.

The majorant in (7) touches at `j`. By strict concavity from Section 5,
it cannot touch at any other feasible base: equality at two bases
would contradict strict concavity on the segment between them and
the fact that (7) majorizes the whole segment. In particular its
right side is strictly positive at every feasible base, including
those with singleton sections. Compactness of `Q_t` makes its minimum
there positive. Equivalently,

    max_(j' in Q_t) bar a.(j'-j) < d.

This interpretation does not imply `bar a=0` at a maximum over
INTEGER bases, even when the candidates are marginally eligible.
Only an appropriate unconstrained real-base optimality statement
could impose such a conclusion, and none is assumed here.
